newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.N. documents torture at Cambodian detention site.
newsitem.headline: U.N. documents torture at Cambodian detention site.

text.p: Thirty soldiers captured in the aftermath of a bloody Cambodian coup two weeks ago were tortured and forced to drink sewer water while under detention by government authorities, United Nations officials said on Sunday.
"We have evidence which is irrefutable of systematic torture at a place called Kambol," a U.N. official, who asked not to be identified by name, told reporters.

"The prisoners were blindfolded and had their hands tied behind their backs for questioning. When (their captors) didn't get the answer they asked for, the prisoners were beaten with sticks, belts and the leg of a table," the official said.

The U.N. said its information was based on direct, individual interviews with eight of 30 prisoners who had been held at Kambol military police training centre adjacent to Pochentong airport, west of Phnom Penh.
The 30 soldiers, loyal to ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, were held in a room two by six metres (six feet by 20 feet) square without adequate light or ventilation.
"They had to sleep standing up and we were told people regularly fell unconscious from the heat and dehydration," the U.N. official said.
The only water the prisoners were given at Kambol came from a sewage pond.
"They said the water smelled and tasted of faecal matter. Some were forced to drink it while under questioning," the U.N. official said.
"The people we spoke to were severely traumatised, some were just in a daze."
He said some prisoners had fingers put in a metal clamp and squeezed when their interrogators considered answers unacceptable.
The U.N. said some of the men, who were interviewed on Friday, still had marks on their fingers.
Others had marks and bruises on their backs from beatings the week before.
The men were interviewed at another detention site, where they were sent for a week of "re-education".

Cambodia's First Prime Minister, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, was ousted from power and his troops routed by troops loyal to Cambodia's new strongman, Hun Sen, during two days of fighting on July 5-6 in Phnom Penh.
About 60 people, including civilians were killed in the street battles and another 200 were wounded.

In addition, rights workers have documented what they say are 40 cases of extrajudicial murder in the wake of the coup. The victims were military, police and government officials loyal to Prince Ranariddh.

A number of opposition figures have gone missing and their whereabouts are unknown. Among them are veteran politician Pen Sovann, who had mooted the possibility of allying his fledgling political party with the Prince.
Sovann has not been seen since July 5, the first day of the fighting in Phnom Penh. Unconfirmed rumours of his death were circulating in the capital.
"We are investigating his disappearance," said a rights worker.
Rights officials say that while there have been no confirmed cases of extrajudicial killings during the past week there was no guarantee some may not have occurred.
"All the killings (we know about) relate to the first week after the coup. They may continue but we simply don't know," a rights worker said.
"It is hard for us to know about what has happened to potentially hundreds of people captured after the fighting."

Rights workers on Sunday showed reporters photographs of a young man with his hands handcuffed behind his back who had been shot in the back of the head. His body was found in a field outside Phnom Penh and remains unidentified.
